::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Half your grade is team-based, and when employers were asked in 2026
what they value in graduates, **communication came first** and
problem-solving second. They also said fewer than half of recent
graduates arrive well-prepared on grit, emotional intelligence, or
managing people.

So this page is not a nicety. It is a short toolkit, with sources, for
the part of the course that most often goes wrong.
:::

## The four things that actually go wrong

Across every capstone course, the same four:

1. **Nobody wrote down who does what**, so the conscientious person does
   it all and resents it by October.
2. **A deadline slips and nothing happens**, because there was no agreed
   consequence and no one wants to be the person who raises it.
3. **The team never says the hard thing** --- that the question is
   vague, that the data is not going to arrive --- because it is easier
   not to.
4. **Everyone finds out in November** that the split of work was uneven,
   when it is too late to fix.

Everything below is aimed at one of those four.

## Tools worth using

### The ground rules, and RACI

You write ground rules in meeting 2. The part teams skip is the **split
of work**, and the standard tool for it is a **RACI matrix** --- for
each task, who is *Responsible* (does it), *Accountable* (one person,
owns whether it happened), *Consulted*, and *Informed*.

It sounds bureaucratic for a five-person team. It takes fifteen minutes
and it prevents failure 1 and failure 4, because "Accountable" is a
single named person for every deliverable.

### The weekly check-in

Ten minutes at the start of every session B: what you did, what is
stuck, who does what next. In writing, handed in.

This is a **stand-up**, borrowed from agile practice, and its purpose
here is not ceremony --- it is that the written record makes an uneven
split visible in week 4 rather than week 13. See Derby & Larsen,
*Agile Retrospectives* (2006), for the family of practices it belongs
to.

### The decision log

One shared document. Every time the team decides something --- the
question, the outcome variable, the data source --- one line: **what was
decided, when, and why.**

Costs nothing, and it is the single best defence against the November
conversation that begins "I thought we agreed...". It also becomes the
spine of your work plan, because a decision log read backwards *is* a
methods section.

### Psychological safety

The best-evidenced finding in this whole area: teams perform better when
members believe they can say something wrong, or admit they are lost,
without being punished for it. That is **psychological safety**, from
Amy Edmondson's work --- *Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in
Work Teams*, Administrative Science Quarterly (1999), and her book *The
Fearless Organization* (2018). Google's internal Project Aristotle study
found it the strongest predictor of team effectiveness among the factors
it examined.

The practical version for a five-person team: **the person who says "I
don't understand what we're doing" is doing the team a favour.** Say so
out loud in meeting 2, and then behave as if it is true.

### Conflict, when it comes

Fisher & Ury, *Getting to Yes* (1981), is the standard reference, and
its central move is the useful one here: **argue about interests, not
positions.** "I want to use this dataset" is a position. "I want us to
finish on time and I don't trust the other source to arrive" is an
interest, and interests can be traded.

Your ground rules should already say when a disagreement comes to me.
Use it earlier than feels comfortable.

## What we will use to assess it

Peer evaluation runs twice, at meetings 6 and 13, on **CATME** --- the
Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member Effectiveness, developed at
Purdue and used by around 17,000 instructors at 2,200 institutions. It
scores five dimensions that research has found matter: contributing to
the team's work, interacting with teammates, keeping the team on track,
expecting quality, and having the relevant knowledge and skills.

See Loughry, Ohland & Moore, *Educational and Psychological Measurement*
(2007), and Ohland et al., *Academy of Management Learning & Education*
(2012).

Two things follow. Your rating of your teammates is **not** a formality
--- it adjusts individual grades on team work. And the five dimensions
are published, so you know in advance what you are being rated on. Read
them in week 1 and behave accordingly.

## Frameworks you will hear about — and what they are worth

Business school will hand you several of these. They are not equally
supported, and knowing which is which is itself part of the course.

| Framework | What it says | What it is worth |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Psychological safety** (Edmondson) | Teams do better when it is safe to be wrong out loud | **Strong.** Extensively replicated, and the mechanism is clear |
| **CATME dimensions** (Ohland et al.) | Five measurable facets of member effectiveness | **Strong.** Validated instrument, large samples |
| **Conditions for team effectiveness** (Haas & Mortensen, HBR 2016) | Compelling direction, strong structure, supportive context, shared mindset | **Good.** Practitioner synthesis of a real literature |
| **Tuckman's stages** — forming, storming, norming, performing (1965) | Teams pass through predictable phases | **Useful vocabulary, weak evidence.** Teams do not reliably move in that order. Use it to name what is happening, not to predict |
| **Belbin team roles** (1981) | Nine roles; balance them | **Popular, poorly supported.** The psychometrics have not held up well. Treat as a conversation starter, not a diagnosis |

That last row is worth pausing on. **A framework being widely used in
business is not evidence that it works** --- which is the same lesson as
the rest of this course, applied to management rather than to data.

- Ohland, M. et al. (2012), "The Comprehensive Assessment of Team Member
